summary30s: The critical edition of the Mahabharata was initiated in 1919 under V.S. Sukthankar, taking 47 years to collate over 13,000 pages from Sanskrit manuscripts across India.
The epic portrays patriliny as the ideal kinship structure, though matrilineal naming practices existed among southern dynasties like the Satavahanas.
Brahmanical texts defined 4 Varnas with divine origin (Purusha Sukta) and occupational prescriptions, while Jatis were flexible social categories not restricted to four.
Gender governed property: paternal estate went to sons with a special share for the eldest; women could only hold Stridhana (gifts at marriage), not immovable property.
Buddhism rejected the divine origin of caste, proposing in the Sutta Pitaka a social contract theory (Mahasammata: the Great Elect).

coreConcepts.title: The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata (1919-1966)
coreConcepts.explanation: In 1919, under the leadership of noted Indian Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar, a mammoth project began to prepare a Critical Edition of the Mahabharata. Scholars collected Sanskrit manuscripts in various scripts (Kashmiri, Bengali, Devanagari, Telugu, Malayalam, Grantha). They selected verses common to all versions. Published in 13,000 pages across numerous volumes, it took 47 years to complete. It revealed two things: striking common elements in the Sanskrit text across the subcontinent, and vast regional variations (recorded in footnotes and appendices, occupying more than half the pages).
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 1
coreConcepts.examTip: CUET checks numbers: 1919 start year, V.S. Sukthankar team leader, 47 years duration, 13,000 pages.

coreConcepts.title: Gotra Rules and Satavahana Exceptions
coreConcepts.explanation: From c. 1000 BCE, people were classified into Gotras named after Vedic seers. Two major rules: (1) Women had to give up their father's gotra and adopt that of their husband upon marriage, and (2) Members of the same gotra could not marry (gotra exogamy). However, Satavahana inscriptions show marked exceptions: Satavahana queens retained their fathers' gotras (e.g., Gotami and Vashithi), and marriages within the same gotra (gotra endogamy) were practiced among kinfolk in South India. Moreover, Satavahana rulers were metronymic (named after mothers: Gautamiputra Satakarni), though succession to the throne remained patrilineal.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 2
coreConcepts.examTip: Crucial CUET trap: Satavahana succession was PATRILINEAL even though kings used METRONYMICS (mother's name).

coreConcepts.title: Varna, Jati, and the Marginalized (Chandalas)
coreConcepts.explanation: Varna was strictly fourfold and divinely ordained. Jati, however, had no fixed numerical limit; when Brahmanical authorities encountered communities that did not fit the fourfold varna (e.g., forest dwellers / Nishadas, goldsmiths / Suvarnakaras), they classified them as Jatis. Communities sharing a craft were organized into Shrenis (e.g., Mandasor stone inscription of silk weavers). Those outside the system were branded 'Mlechchhas' (barbarians). At the very bottom were 'Untouchables' or Chandalas, whose duties according to the Manusmriti included: living outside the village, using discarded utensils, wearing clothes of the dead, ornaments of iron, and disposing of unclaimed corpses.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 3
coreConcepts.examTip: Chinese pilgrim Fa Xian (5th century CE) noted that 'untouchables' had to clap clappers when entering streets so people could avoid seeing them; Xuan Zang noted scavengers were forced to live outside city walls.

coreConcepts.title: Gendered Access to Property & Buddhist Social Contract
coreConcepts.explanation: According to the Manusmriti, the paternal estate was to be divided equally among sons after the death of the parents, with a special share for the eldest. Women were not entitled to claim a share of these ancestral resources. However, women could retain gifts received at their marriage as 'Stridhana' (woman's wealth), which could be inherited by their children without the husband having a claim. In contrast, the Buddhist text Sutta Pitaka suggested that initially humans lived in an idyllic state, but with deterioration and greed, people chose an individual through consensus to maintain order in exchange for a share of rice: the 'Mahasammata' (the Great Elect). This was an early social contract theory, rejecting divine creation.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 4 & 5
coreConcepts.examTip: Remember the term 'Mahasammata' - the Great Elect chosen by the people in Buddhist philosophy.

workedExamples.question:
Which of the following Chinese Buddhist travellers wrote that 'untouchables' (Chandalas) had to sound a clapper in the streets so that people could avoid seeing them?
(A) Xuan Zang
(B) Fa Xian
(C) I-Qing
(D) Faxian and Xuan Zang together in a joint chronicle
workedExamples.explanation: According to NCERT Theme 1 Chapter 3, the Chinese Buddhist monk Fa Xian (who visited India c. 5th century CE) wrote that 'untouchables' had to sound a clapper in the streets so that people could avoid seeing them, which was believed to be polluting. Xuan Zang (7th century CE) observed that executioners and scavengers were forced to live outside that city.
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Fa Xian (5th century CE) -> recorded the striking of clapper/piece of wood upon entering streets.
Step 2: Xuan Zang (7th century CE) -> recorded executioners and scavengers living outside city gates.
Conclusion: Option B (Fa Xian) is the precise historical attribution.
workedExamples.cuetPattern: Differentiating between Fa Xian's and Xuan Zang's observations on caste pollution.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Fa Xian (5th century CE) -> recorded the striking of clapper/piece of wood upon entering streets.
Step 2: Xuan Zang (7th century CE) -> recorded executioners and scavengers living outside city gates.
Conclusion: Option B (Fa Xian) is the precise historical attribution.

workedExamples.question:
The famous Mandasor inscription (Madhya Pradesh) records the history of a guild of:
(A) Silk weavers who migrated from Lata (Gujarat)
(B) Ivory carvers of Vidisha who funded Sanchi toranas
(C) Blacksmiths who forged iron pillars
(D) Horse merchants from the north-west
workedExamples.explanation: A stone inscription found at Mandasor (Madhya Pradesh) records the history of a guild of silk weavers who originally lived in Lata (Gujarat) and migrated to Mandasor (then known as Dashapura) attracted by the fame of the local king.
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Recall the Mandasor inscription (5th century CE).
Step 2: Identifies a guild (shreni) of silk weavers migrating from Lata (Gujarat) to Dashapura (Mandasor).
Step 3: They pooled resources to construct a magnificent temple to the Sun god.
workedExamples.cuetPattern: Direct inscription identification question regarding social mobility of guilds.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Recall the Mandasor inscription (5th century CE).

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: According to Manusmriti, which of the following is true regarding women's right to property?
howCuetAsks.strategy: Women could own Stridhana (gifts at marriage), but could not claim ancestral land or family property.

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics. Did this mean society was matriarchal?
howCuetAsks.strategy: No, succession was patrilineal; only royal names included the mother's gotra (e.g. Gautamiputra).

commonTraps.misconception: Assuming the Mahabharata critical edition was compiled from just a few Sanskrit manuscripts in north India.
commonTraps.correctConcept: It collated hundreds of manuscripts written on palm leaf and paper in various regional scripts (Kashmiri, Devanagari, Bengali, Telugu, Malayalam, Grantha) across North and South India.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Questions ask whether south Indian manuscripts were included; they were thoroughly included.
commonTraps.cuetWarning: The critical edition proved both pan-Indian unity and tremendous regional variations.

commonTraps.correctConcept: Varna is strictly four (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra). Jati has no fixed number and accommodates new occupational groups, tribes, and foreigners.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Options say 'There were 16 Varnas and 4 Jatis' or similar inversions.

quickRevisionCard.title: Kinship, Caste and Class Quick Revision
bulletPoints: Mahabharata Critical Edition: Started 1919 by V.S. Sukthankar; took 47 years, 13,000 pages.
Patriliny: Traced from father to son; Mahabharata war fought between cousins (Kauravas and Pandavas) over land and power.
Gotra Rules: Brahmanical code required exogamy and changing woman's gotra to husband's upon marriage.
Satavahana Rulers: Practiced gotra endogamy, queens retained father's gotra, metronymic titles used, but succession was patrilineal.
Varna vs Jati: 4 Varnas fixed by birth; Jatis unlimited (e.g., Nishadas, Suvarnakaras).
Mandasor Inscription: 5th-century guild of silk weavers who migrated from Lata (Gujarat) to Dashapura.
Manusmriti on Chandalas: Lived outside village, used broken pots, wore dead clothes, touched corpses.
Stridhana: Gifts given to woman during marriage; her absolute right inherited by children.
Polyandry: Draupadi married to five Pandavas; recognized as a variant form of marriage in early India.
Buddhist View: Sutta Pitaka explains social inequality via 'Mahasammata' (elected king via social contract).

practiceQuestions.question: Under whose leadership was the ambitious project of preparing the Critical Edition of the Mahabharata initiated in 1919?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In 1919, the renowned Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar led a team of scholars to prepare the Critical Edition of the Mahabharata.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following dynasties provides historical evidence of rulers practicing endogamy (marriage within the kin unit/gotra) contrary to Brahmanical rules?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Satavahana rulers married women who belonged to the same gotra, illustrating endogamous marriage practices prevalent in parts of South India.

practiceQuestions.question: According to the Dharmashastras, what was the term used for wealth received by a woman during her marriage that could be inherited by her children?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gifts given to a bride during her marriage were called 'stridhana' (literally, woman's wealth), which could be inherited by children without the husband having a claim.

practiceQuestions.question: In the Buddhist text Sutta Pitaka, the king who was elected by the whole people to maintain social order was designated as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Sutta Pitaka suggests people chose someone who would be capable of dispensing justice: he was known as 'Mahasammata', the Great Elect.

practiceQuestions.question: B.B. Lal excavated the village of Hastinapura in Meerut (U.P.) in 1951-52. What was the distinctive ceramic type found in Period II associated with early epic traditions?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Period II at Hastinapura (c. 12th-7th centuries BCE) yielded Painted Grey Ware (PGW), mud-brick walls, and reed thatch structures.

practiceQuestions.question: According to the Manusmriti, which of the following was NOT a duty prescribed for the Chandalas?

options.text: They had to live outside the village
They had to wear ornaments of iron and clothes of the dead
They could enter villages at night to purchase grain
They had to serve as executioners and dispose of corpses of those without relatives

practiceQuestions.explanation: The Manusmriti explicitly stated that Chandalas could NOT walk about in villages and cities at night; they had to stay outside.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following forms of marriage involves a woman having multiple husbands simultaneously, as seen in the case of Draupadi?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Polyandry is the practice of a woman having several husbands. Draupadi's marriage to the five Pandavas is the most famous example in ancient Indian literature.

practiceQuestions.question: The story of Matanga, a Bodhisatta born as a Chandala who married Dittha Mangalika, is found in which of the following Buddhist Jatakas?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Matanga Jataka tells the story of the Bodhisatta born outside the city as an outcaste Chandala named Matanga.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Satavahana kings used metronymics, yet their system of dynastic succession was patrilineal.
Reason (R): In the Satavahana kingdom, royal authority and the throne passed from father to son, despite rulers bearing names derived from their mothers like Gautamiputra.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: While Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics (names derived from mothers), succession to the throne was almost generally patrilineal (passed from father to son). Both are true and (R) explains (A).

practiceQuestions.question: Which category of texts in ancient India defined the 'Dharma' or ideal conduct for the four varnas?
practiceQuestions.explanation: From c. 500 BCE, Brahmanas compiled Sanskrit legal codes known as the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras (most notable being the Manusmriti).
